questions.question: Quick Sort uses the LAST element as pivot. Which input causes worst-case behavior: an already-sorted array, or a randomly shuffled array?
questions.solutionApproach: With last-element pivot on already-sorted input, the last (largest) element is always the pivot, giving a 0-vs-(n-1) split every time — worst case O(n²). Random shuffle gives roughly balanced splits on average.
questions.answer: Already-sorted array causes worst-case O(n²) behavior with last-element pivot.

questions.question: A pivot-selection method guarantees a split where each side gets at least n/10 elements. What is the resulting worst-case complexity?
questions.solutionApproach: T(n) = T(n/10) + T(9n/10) + Θ(n). This is a fixed-ratio split (not depending on n), so it still resolves to Θ(n log n) — just with a larger constant than balanced 50-50 splits.
questions.answer: Θ(n log n) — any fixed-ratio split, even 1:9, still gives n log n.

questions.question: In randomized Quick Sort on 20 distinct elements, what is the probability the pivot in the first partition ends up at the worst possible position (index 1 or index n)?
questions.solutionApproach: Worst position happens iff pivot value = min or max. 2 favorable values out of 20 total. P = 2/20 = 0.1.

questions.question: Array [3,7,1,9,2] with Lomuto partition using the LAST element (2) as pivot. What is the array after this one partition step, and what's the pivot's final index (0-indexed)?
questions.solutionApproach: Lomuto: i=-1. j=0(3): 3>2, no swap. j=1(7): 7>2, no swap. j=2(1): 1≤2, i=0, swap a[0],a[2] → [1,7,3,9,2]. j=3(9): 9>2, no swap. End loop, swap a[i+1]=a[1] with pivot a[4]: swap → [1,2,3,9,7]. Pivot (2) now at index 1.
